Part 01 · Overview

Keep a sale and an operating plan both ready, and choose on 22 January.

Sleep Media is the one profitable business under a senior loan of $103.1M, and its search revenue fell 23% this year to August. The plan is one standstill to 31 March 2027, a sale process run by a banker, and an operating plan tested by people who did not write it. The readings that separate the paths arrive by 15 January, and on 22 January a rule fixed in advance picks one.

A sale is the default, and three readings could change the answer.

The no-renewal case also has click-outs of 28,500 a week against 32,000, other revenue of $2.4M against $3.0M, and a buyer paying 3.0 times earnings against 3.5. Google clicks are 26% below the summer average, and the click-out count for November has not been seen. The value Comvest showed for the loan on 30 September is $13.7M.

Part 02 · Situation

Sleep Media earns the money, Sleep Care spends it, and the loan's deadlines are close.

This part sets out what the company's own records show: the two businesses, the debt, the dates, the cash, the search revenue that Sleep Media lives on and the sites it competes with. Actual figures run to August 2026, and later months are management's forecast. The record is read against last year, and not against budget.

Sleep Media earns the money, and Sleep Care and head office spend more.

OneCare Media trades as Sleep Doctor and runs two businesses inside one borrower. Sleep Media publishes sleepfoundation.org and earns a commission when a reader clicks through to a seller. Sleep Care sells home sleep apnea tests and CPAP breathing machines, for cash and since 2026 through insurance.

What holds. Sleep Media earns about $13M before shared costs on management's forecast. Standing on its own, it earned about $8.7M over the twelve months to August.

What to watch. Sleep Care and head office together spend about $17M, so the company as a whole loses money.

Sources: long-range plan of 21 October 2026.

The debt is many times what the business is worth.

The senior loan was $100.6M in September 2026 and reaches $103.1M in December as unpaid interest is added to it. Comvest holds about 58.9% of it, a claim of $60.7M. Falcon holds $85.9M of junior notes that rank behind the senior loan. On each case in this packet the value reaches the senior loan and nothing below it.

What holds. The senior lenders are the only parties with money still at stake, which gives them the standing to set terms.

What to watch. Comvest's share is from an April 2024 list, and the current list of lenders has not been seen.

The loan's own deadlines fall inside the nineteen weeks to closing.

Until 30 November 2026 interest is added to the loan in place of being paid. After that it falls due in cash, at about $0.9M a month. A test that the company holds $2.5M of cash runs monthly to 28 February 2027, and a test of $2.0M of earnings falls on 31 March 2027. The first cash interest, about $0.91M, is due at the turn of the year, and the lenders can act if it is not paid by 6 January 2027.

What holds. The company cannot pass these tests on its own forecast, so it needs the lenders' patience, and patience can carry conditions.

What to watch. The loan documents themselves have not been seen. The amount, the default date and the $2.5M level come from the lenders' call of 20 November.

Cash has fallen for two years and now rests on a domain sale.

The company forecasts $2.85M of cash for 27 November, of which $1.9M came from selling a web domain in January. Average cash was $10.1M in October 2024 and $3.2M in September 2026.

What holds. The company's forecast stays above the $2.5M test to 1 January, before any cost of change or any cash interest.

What to watch. Without a standstill, paying the first interest of about $0.91M takes the forecast's $2.98M on 1 January to about $2.07M, below the test, unless costs fall first. Receipts missed the two latest forecasts, and no bank statement has been seen.

Search revenue fell by nearly a quarter this year, despite a higher price per click.

Sleep Foundation's search revenue was $8.0M from January to August 2026, against $10.4M a year earlier, a fall of 23%. Google clicks were 975K in October against 1,874K a year earlier. Revenue fell less than clicks, because a larger share of readers clicked through to a seller and each click earned more under the largest partner's guaranteed price.

What holds. The falls since March are smaller than in the winter: about half in January, and about 17% in July and August.

What to watch. April and May came within 7% of a year earlier, and the gap has widened again since June. The guaranteed price expires on 31 December, and management's forecast needs search revenue from September to December to run 33% above a year earlier.

Sources: long-range plan of 21 October 2026, organic revenue sheet.

Against last year, the third quarter fell where the company reports it steady.

The company's board pre-read reads the third quarter against a budget that was cut after May, and calls it back on plan. Against the same months of 2025, revenue that depends on Google fell from $4.83M to $3.48M, down 28%. All Sleep Media revenue fell 12%, from $4.97M to $4.36M.

What holds. Revenue that does not depend on Google, which is advertising, AI referrals, video and e-mail, rose from $0.14M to $0.88M.

What to watch. The two company sources do not fully reconcile, and neither is checked against partner statements.

Sources: Q3 2026 board pre-read, pages 13 and 14.

Google clicks are about a quarter below the summer level, and still edging down.

Google sent 198K clicks to sleepfoundation.org in the week of 9 November, against a summer average of 267K a week. That is 26% lower. Clicks fell 18% in the six weeks from late September, with the largest single drop in the week of 12 October. Each full week since has been lower than the one before.

What holds. The best-of pages have been level since mid-October, at about 41K to 42K clicks a week on this export and the plan's earlier ones. The first three days of the week of 16 November were 5% above the same days a week earlier.

What to watch. Click-outs to sellers start on the best-of pages. The base case needs about 32,000 a week, and the no-renewal case uses 28,500. The company's weekly click-out figure for November has not been seen.

The pages where readers click through to sellers fell more than the rest. The 312 best-of pages averaged 5.8K clicks a day from 22 October to 19 November, against 9.0K in July, a fall of 36%. The rest of the site fell 24%. The fall is in the United States and Australia, each down about a third, and the United Kingdom is level.

Sleep Foundation leads its field on visits and trust, and lags on proof of testing.

The competitive set is the sites that rank for the same mattress and sleep terms, read from a third-party tracker on 17 November 2026. Sleep Foundation draws about 2.0M search visits a month, about three times its nearest rival. Four of the rival review sites belong to Pillar4 Media, which this packet names as the likeliest buyer.

What holds. Sleep Foundation scores highest on links, medical review and appearances in AI answers, which are the hardest strengths for a rival to copy.

What to watch. Specialist sites that publish their own test results took mattress rankings from the large publishers after May 2025. Sleep Foundation scores lower on proof of testing, and that is where a rival gains.

The sale price is close to the earlier packet's, and the path has changed.

The packet of 10 November 2026 valued Sleep Media as a business before debt, over five years. This packet values what Comvest can collect, after costs, the other lenders and the wait. The base case keeps that packet's reading that the partner's guaranteed price carries on, and starts 2027 with the same search revenue, so the sale price is close to it. Both packets rest on the same company records for Sleep Media, all dated before 10 November. The new information since is two more weeks of Google clicks and a newer filing for the mark. The rest is method: what reaches Comvest is counted in place of the value of the business, improvements count where a tested plan shows them, and the cost and new money of a takeover are counted.

What holds. The debt, the $5.6M cost of running Sleep Media on its own, the 15% rate and the range of 3.0 to 3.5 times earnings are unchanged. So is the weight on next year's partner terms, which the earlier packet called the top priority.

What to watch. The base case of $30.2M needs signed terms and click-outs holding near 32,000 a week. Neither reading is known yet, and without renewal the sale price is $14.8M.

The sale side. The earlier packet put a managed sale at $32M to $37M, or about $29M after selling cost and the wait. The base case here is $30.2M, and $25.6M reaches the four lenders. The step that is new is Comvest's share.

The holding side. The earlier packet valued a five-year harvest at about $45M, against about $29M for a sale. It said about $13M of that came from ten improvements, counted at a risk-weighted value. With none of them the same harvest was $31.7M, which is about $3M above a sale, before any cost of taking ownership. This packet shows the improvements as a plan to be tested, and counts those costs.

What holds. The earlier packet's conclusion still has its counterpart here. With search holding and the full plan landing, operating returns $36.9M to the four lenders, against $25.6M from a sale.

What to watch. The earlier packet named a further step-down in clicks on commercial pages after the holiday quarter as its trigger to sell. Clicks on the best-of pages are 36% below July, and most of that fall came before 10 November. They have been level since mid-October, so the trigger is not met. Decision day on 22 January falls after that quarter.

Part 03 · Scenarios and logic

December readings pick the sale case, and a fixed rule picks the path.

This part sets out how value is built, how a price becomes cash to Comvest, the four sale cases and the severe case, and the three paths after decision day. Each sale case is a sale that closes on 31 March 2027. No odds and no blended value are shown, because the readings that pick the case arrive by 31 December.

Value is built from clicks to sellers, what each earns, cost and a buyer's price.

A click-out is a click from a Sleep Foundation page through to a seller, and it is the unit that earns commission. Search revenue is weekly click-outs times 52 times revenue per click-out. Revenue per click-out divides search revenue from every site by Sleep Foundation's click-outs, so the January to August figure of $5.73 is a little above the $5.40 that Sleep Foundation alone earned per click-out. The base case uses $7.02, the August figure under the partner's guaranteed price. Other revenue is added, the cost of running Sleep Media on its own is taken off, and a buyer pays a number of years of the earnings that result.

What holds. The model was built from two separate analyses of the same records, and it reproduces each of their values before any input is changed.

What to watch. No input rests on a bank statement, a signed loan document, a supplier's quote or an offer.

A price reaches the four lenders in proportion, and then Comvest.

On the base case a price of $30.2M leaves about $25.6M for the four lenders and about $15.1M for Comvest, in today's money. The price first pays the selling cost and the costs the old company leaves behind. Those leftover costs are $1.75M on the base case: the $0.76M cash gap at closing, which the new money has covered, and $1.0M of later costs for tax, priority claims and the wind-up. What is left is put in today's money, which means reduced for the wait at 15% a year. It goes to the four senior lenders in proportion to their share of the loan: Comvest 58.87%, Vistria Credit 26.76%, Cliffwater 9.3%, Pantheon 5.1%.

What holds. Keeping the money already owed to the company with the seller is worth about $0.7M to Comvest, for one line on the bid form.

What to watch. Offers are likely to include a part paid later. A quarter of the price paid that way costs Comvest about $2.1M on the base case.

The readings that pick the sale case arrive by 31 December.

Two questions pick the case. Are 2027 partner terms signed, in a form that carries over to a new owner, by 31 December? Do weekly click-outs hold at 27,000 or more after Google's update? A fall below 21,000 a week for two weeks is the severe case, in which a sale has no value to the lenders and the site is run off for cash.

What holds. Signed terms with lower click-outs return more to Comvest than unsigned terms with click-outs holding.

What to watch. Weekly click-outs were last matched for August, and no count for November has been seen.

The three paths differ in who owns Sleep Media, and for how long.

The work to 22 January is the same whatever happens next: a standstill, a sale process run by a banker, and an operating plan tested by people who did not write it. A sale ends the lenders' involvement in March. Ownership keeps it for up to two years and needs more new money first. The exhibit sets out what each path needs to be true, what the record says today, and when each point will be known.

What holds. The first 60 days are the same on each path, so nothing is given up by keeping all three open.

What to watch. The point that matters most for operating, the yearly fall in search revenue after 2027, is not known by decision day. The first review is on 30 September 2027.

A sale rests on public price evidence and on buyers not yet approached.

No offer has been seen, and buyers are approached from 14 December. The base case's price of 3.5 times next-year earnings is above what listed publishers and brokered sites fetch, on the view that a buyer pays more for signed partner terms. Listed publishers that depend on search trade at about 3 times earnings, and brokered content sites sell at 2.0 to 2.8 times annual profit. A 2026 broker guide gives 3 to 10 times annual earnings for private site sales, with content sites in the lower to middle part.

What holds. The likeliest buyer already owns five rival sites, so it knows the traffic risk and can price it.

What to watch. Buyers answer search exposure with a lower price, a part of the price tied to later results or an amount held back. A part paid later is valued at no more than half.

Operating rests on holding search with a smaller team and new revenue.

The plan protects what earns the money and changes cost by stages. The site's rankings rest on product testing and medical review, so those stay funded. AI tools are proved on about 50 pages before any role changes, and the team steps down to six over the first year. Six revenue ideas make up a target of $1.5M a year by late 2028, each run as a 30-day test with a budget and one owner.

What holds. Separating Sleep Media from head office removes far more cost than AI does, and that saving arrives on any path.

What to watch. A tenth of search revenue is worth more than the whole AI saving, so the roles that protect revenue are the last to change. The core of six is not quoted, and none of the six revenue ideas is contracted.

An offer has to beat what the lenders can show ownership would return.

The lenders sell unless owning beats the best offer by the greater of $1.0M and 10% of the value of owning. The minimum price is the offer below which they do better by owning, after that margin. If ownership means collecting cash from a shrinking business it is about $18.0M. If a tested plan shows search revenue holding it is about $31.4M, and about $34.8M with the team down to six.

What holds. A close call goes to the cash offer. An offer counts if it has proof of funds, a stated structure and a closing on or before 31 March.

What to watch. The operating plan is tested by the independent officer and the banker, who did not write it. Without a tested plan, ownership is valued as collecting cash.

How the rule runs. The readings that pick the case arrive by 31 December, and the offers and the tested plan by 15 January. On 22 January three questions turn them into a path.

Test the rule. Three things are known by the middle of January: what the December readings show, the best offer for Sleep Media, and what the tested operating plan shows. Choose an answer to each, and the explorer gives the path the rule picks, what it is worth to Comvest and what happens next. It opens on the base case, with a fair offer and search revenue holding. The grid under it shows the whole rule on the base case. If click-outs collapse, any offer is compared with a run-off instead.

Part 04 · Outcomes

A March sale on the base case returns a little more than the September mark.

This part sets what Comvest gets back in each scenario against the value it showed for the loan on 30 September: 22.5 cents per dollar, or $13.7M. Each figure is Comvest's share on the same $60.7M claim, in today's money, after the new money is repaid first. The mark is an accounting value and not a bid, so an indicative offer for the loan is the market test.

The base sale clears the value Comvest showed in September, and no renewal halves it.

Comvest carried the loan at 22.5 cents per dollar on 30 September 2026, which is $13.7M on its claim. A sale on the base case returns about $15.1M, or 24.8 cents. It is the one sale case that clears the mark. If the partner's price does not renew, a sale returns $6.7M, or 11.1 cents.

What holds. The comparison is like for like: the same claim, Comvest's share alone, and cash after the new money is repaid.

What to watch. The scenario values are discounted at 15% a year to 19 November 2026, and the mark is a value at 30 September. A mark is the holder's own estimate, and no buyer has put a price on the loan.

Part 05 · Sensitivities

The choice turns on whether search revenue keeps falling after 2027.

This part shows what moves each result most. A sale turns on click-outs, revenue per click-out and the price a buyer pays. Operating turns on what search revenue does after 2027, and its break-even is set against the company's own record.

The partner's price not renewing moves the base case more than any other input.

Each test changes one input on the base case and holds the rest. The base case already has click-outs at the summer level and the partner's price at the August high, so the two revenue inputs are shown as falls. The last row is the whole no-renewal case, which lowers four inputs together and takes $8.3M from Comvest's value.

What holds. Each of the largest gains is something the plan works on directly: partner terms, a new owner for Sleep Care, the bid form and a quoted budget.

What to watch. The changes do not simply add up, because click-outs and revenue per click-out multiply. These rows were computed for this packet with the plan's sale arithmetic, and the cost of a late closing was not measured on this base.

The partner's price is the largest single input. The no-renewal case lowers four inputs at once. Taken one at a time, the price per click-out comes first, then click-outs, other revenue and the price a buyer pays.

Holding search revenue matters more than the rest of the plan together.

Moving from falling to steady search adds about $8.4M for Comvest. The smaller team adds about $2.0M and the new revenue about $2.3M. The smaller team is a core of six people with tested AI tools at about $4.5M a year, and the new revenue is a target of $1.5M a year by late 2028.

What holds. Separating Sleep Media from head office removes far more cost than AI does, and that saving arrives on any path.

What to watch. A tenth of search revenue is worth more than the whole AI saving. The core of six is not quoted, and none of the six revenue ideas is contracted.

The break-even for operating is a small yearly fall in search.

On today's team, ownership equals a March sale when search revenue falls by about 6% a year after 2027 and a later buyer pays the same 3.5 times earnings. Once the team is down to six, the break-even is a fall of about 10% a year. If the full plan lands it is about 16%, and the sale cases assume 15%.

What holds. The break-even is about the years after 2027. The base case already starts that year about 3% below the last twelve months.

What to watch. After the margin the rule asks for, operating has to do better still: a fall of no more than about 2% a year on today's team, a fall of no more than about 6% a year on a core of six, and about 12% with the full plan.

The company's record is a faster fall than any break-even.

Search revenue fell 26% from 2024 to 2025 and 23% in the first eight months of 2026, and revenue that depends on Google fell 28% from July to September. At 20% to 25% a year after 2027, ownership on a core of six returns $9.7M to $11.4M against $15.1M from a sale. Operating is a bet that the fall slows sharply from 2028.

What holds. The falls since March are smaller than in the winter: about half in January, 4% in April and about 17% in July and August.

What to watch. Even if the full plan lands, the break-even is a fall of about 16% a year, which is slower than the record.

Five stop rules end the path before losses build.

The path is a bet that search revenue can be held, and each rule names a reading that shows the bet is going wrong. The first review is on 30 September 2027. If search keeps falling and the lenders stop there, Comvest gets back about $9.6M to $11.5M, against $9.1M by carrying on.

The five rules are click-outs collapsing, search revenue falling more than 10% below the case for a quarter, the new company's cash, the largest partner's terms, and the plan's own stages. The supporting evidence sets each out with its trigger.

What holds. The business is kept ready for sale throughout, so stopping takes weeks and not months.

What to watch. Trying and stopping still costs about $3.6M to $5.5M against a sale in March, and about $6.7M if the fall is fast.

Part 06 · What it takes

Each path needs new money first, and most decisions fall before 11 December.

This part sets out the new money each path needs, the timetable, the decisions asked of Comvest with their dates, the conditions for operating, and what has not been checked at source.

Holding the cash test to March needs about $3.3M of new money.

Cash falls from $2.85M on 30 November to below zero by 31 March on the base case, before any funding. Holding the $2.5M test at each month end needs about $3.3M, which is $0.50M more than the plan's $2.0M floor. A partner paying $0.6M in advance, a domain sale that already has an offer, and a new owner for Sleep Care by 31 January bring the need to about $0.9M. The plan asks the lenders to commit up to $3.5M in two instalments. A $3.0M credit line already exists, and counsel is asked whether it can carry most of the money.

What holds. The money is repaid first, ahead of the existing loan, and is paid out against an agreed budget. Comvest's share of the base need is about $1.9M.

What to watch. The advance payment and the domain sale are requests and not receipts. Without a new owner for Sleep Care they leave the need at about $2.5M.

If the lenders own, they fund the costs a sale price would have paid.

In a sale, the price pays the selling cost and the costs the old company leaves behind. If the lenders take ownership there is no price, so they fund those costs, the cost of the transfer and the first weeks of the new company. That comes to about $3.8M before the levers, about $2M more than a sale uses.

What holds. The new company earns about $0.7M a month on the base case, so it is out of the red within three months and repays the lenders from its own cash.

What to watch. Comvest's share would be about $2.2M before the levers, and the money stays out until early 2028 if search holds.

A single route runs to decision day, and three paths follow it.

The standstill is signed on 11 December and runs to 31 March 2027. Buyers are approached from 14 December, written offers are due on 15 January, and decision day is 22 January. A sale then closes on 31 March, and ownership runs to a later sale by mid-2028 or by March 2029.

What holds. A missed date stops further funding or starts the fallback, so the timetable enforces itself.

What to watch. The approach to buyers runs across two holiday weeks. Each month added to a closing costs Comvest $0.4M to $0.6M where the terms do not renew, and the cost was not measured on the base case.

Six conditions come before any choice to operate.

If one condition is unmet, the lenders sell or collect, and do not operate. The lenders set the stop rules, the funding and the final sale. The operator answers to a board of three, with two people named by the lenders and one independent.

What holds. The plan is tested by the independent officer and the banker before the lenders rely on it.

What to watch. Owning past the loan's due date of 31 December 2027 is untested, and counsel's view on it is one of the six conditions.

Sleep Care's loss is its overhead, and a small unit could about break even.

From January to August 2026 at a yearly rate, the paid new-patient funnel lost about $1.2M after its costs, repeat and other sales earned about $1.0M, and overhead was $8.25M. The plan caps paid marketing now and chooses Sleep Care's future by 31 January: a new owner, a small unit that pays its way, or a funded wind-down.

Four weak points bear on the choice. Each is a reading that would move the answer, and each is named so it can be watched.

The base case

Nothing is signed for 2027. If the price does not renew, a sale returns $6.7M to Comvest in place of $15.1M. At 28,500 click-outs a week the base sale returns about $12.8M, below the September mark.

A sale

No offer exists. A price of 3.5 times earnings is above the public evidence of 2.0 to about 3 times, and a weak process could bring about 2.5 times, which returns about $10.5M to Comvest.

Operating

The record shows search revenue falling 23% to 28% a year. The core of six is not quoted, and the revenue plan is a target with no contract behind it.

Owning

The loan falls due on 31 December 2027, nine months after a takeover. Counsel has to confirm how a lender-owned company deals with that date.

Part 07 · Assumptions and method

The numbers rest on stated assumptions, and none is yet checked at source.

Each assumption is written once here and named by its number in the closing line of each exhibit. The sensitivity is the change in Comvest's value for the step shown, with the other inputs held. It is measured where the partner's price does not renew, as the plan's register states it, and part 05 gives the changes on the base case.

Forty-four assumptions carry the figures in this packet.

The numbers are those of the full register behind the plan, so a gap in the sequence is an assumption this packet does not use.

The packet sets out a plan, and it checks nothing at source.

What this packet does

It sets out one route for the senior lenders to decision day and the three paths that follow, with what each is worth, what each needs, the dates and the open items.

What it does not do

It checks nothing against source systems, and it gives no legal, tax or healthcare regulatory advice. It does not set the value Comvest carries in its accounts or the return it requires.

How a sale is valued

Weekly click-outs times 52 times revenue per click-out, plus other revenue, less the cost of running Sleep Media on its own, give earnings for the twelve months from closing. A buyer pays a number of years of those earnings. Selling cost and leftover costs come off, the result is put in today's money at 15% a year, and Comvest takes its 58.9% share.

How ownership is valued

Month by month from April 2027, the new company's earnings build its cash. Cash above $2.0M is paid to the lenders each month. The business is then sold at a stated number of years of the next twelve months' earnings. Each amount is put in today's money at 15% a year.

How the cases are set

Two readings select the sale case: whether 2027 partner terms are signed, and whether click-outs hold at 27,000 a week or more. No odds and no blended value are shown. The base case is the case with terms signed and click-outs holding, which is the reading the packet of 10 November took. The no-renewal view sets the base to the case with terms unsigned.

How the mark is compared

Each scenario is Comvest's share on the same claim of $60.7M, in today's money, after the new money is repaid first. The mark is the value shown on 30 September 2026. It is an accounting value at that date, and not a bid.

Where the models come from

The plan of 19 November printed the sale cases and ran ownership from the no-renewal case. For this packet the same ownership model was run again from the base case, and it reproduces the plan's printed row for that case. The sale model was built from two separate analyses of the same records. The ownership model was built for this work and matched to the sale model's values for owning and collecting, with three inputs set to make them agree. Neither has had an outside review.

The tools

The path explorer applies the decision-day rule to the published values of each case. The two simulators run a simpler version of the models. On the settings of a published case they show the published figures. Elsewhere the value is the simulator's own, from arithmetic that came within $0.1M of each published figure it was checked against. The published cases remain the reference.

The packet of 10 November

Figures quoted from the packet of 10 November 2026 appear where the change is explained, on the Overview and in the Situation part. They are business values before debt, and they are superseded.

Who prepared it

CreditSwan prepared the analysis and may be proposed for a role in carrying it out, under a separate document that nothing in this packet depends on.

Part 08 · FAQ

Most questions turn on evidence that arrives by the middle of January.

The questions a credit committee is likely to ask of this packet, grouped by scope, interpretation, provenance, findings and process. Each answer gives the short version first, then the detail, and names the exhibits that carry the figures.

The packet sets out a plan for the lenders, and checks nothing at source.

A plan for the senior lenders, built from the company's own records and from public sources.

It sets out what to do before the standstill is signed, the route to decision day on 22 January, the three paths that follow, what each costs and what each is worth. It is not a diligence pack: it checks nothing against source systems, and it gives no legal, tax or healthcare regulatory advice. Exhibit 6.09 lists what has to be checked first.

Actual figures run to August 2026, and later months are management's forecast or a case in the models.

Values are in today's money, which means discounted at 15% a year to 19 November 2026. Google clicks run to 18 November from a Search Console export. Exhibit 3.01 builds a sale step by step from weekly click-outs.

Eighteen decisions, most of them before the standstill is signed on 11 December.

The first three need no new money and fall due by 25 November. Exhibit 6.05 lists each decision with its date, and the Decisions section of the Overview links each one to the section that supports it.

The base case assumes the largest partner's guaranteed price renews for 2027, and nothing is signed.

The packet of 10 November valued Sleep Media on earnings that include that price, and the base case keeps to it. The switch at the top of each part shows the whole packet on the other reading, and every figure and chart changes with it. Exhibit 5.02 walks from one reading to the other, one input at a time.

The cases are read from evidence, and no odds are given.

The record does not support odds.

Two readings pick the sale case, and both arrive by 31 December: whether 2027 partner terms are signed, and whether click-outs hold after Google's update. The packet shows the four cases and the severe case in Exhibit 3.03 and Exhibit 3.04, and the evidence that selects between them.

On the base case a March sale returns a little more than the September mark.

Comvest showed $13.7M for the loan on 30 September, at 22.5 cents. A sale on the base case returns $15.1M, and it needs both the renewal and a price of 3.5 times earnings to clear the mark. Without the renewal it returns $6.7M. The mark is a holder's accounting value and not a bid. Exhibit 4.01 sets the scenarios against it, and Exhibit 4.04 shows what a sale would need to match it.

Sellers pay for click-outs, so they are the unit that earns revenue.

Google clicks fell by about half in a year, while revenue fell by less, because a rising share of readers clicked through to a seller. Google clicks are kept as the early warning, in Exhibit 2.07 and Exhibit 2.08. The company's click-out count for November has not been seen.

The legal step is the same, and the plan is different.

Collecting keeps today's team and takes the cash while the business shrinks. Operating adds an operator, a staged cost plan, a revenue plan and stop rules. Exhibit 3.05 sets out what each path needs to be true, and Exhibit 4.02 sets the three side by side.

Each opens on a stated case and shows Comvest's value against a floor.

Each driver has evidence behind its range, set out in Exhibit 5.18. Exhibit 5.03 covers a sale and opens on the base case. Exhibit 5.07 covers ownership and opens on search holding. On the settings of a published case each shows the published figures.

Every figure comes from the company's records, public sources or two models.

Company figures come from the long-range plan, the update to lenders, the monthly packages, the cash forecasts and the Search Console exports.

Sale values come from the recovery model, which was built from two separate analyses of the same records. Ownership values come from a month-by-month model. Each exhibit names its source in its closing line, and each section closes with its sources and the assumptions it rests on.

The signed loan documents, a bank statement and the current list of lenders have not been seen.

Weekly click-outs were last matched for August 2026. No line of cost is quoted, and no offer exists for either business. Exhibit 6.09 lists nine items to check first, with an owner and a date for each.

It reproduces the sale model's values for owning and collecting closely in each case.

Exhibit 5.19 sets the two side by side. Three of its inputs were set to make them agree, and the register lists them. The figures on the base case are a re-run of the same model from case A, and the figures for operating have had no outside review, so the plan asks the independent officer and the banker to test them.

The largest is the renewal of the partner's price.

Without the renewal a March sale returns $6.7M in place of $15.1M, as Exhibit 5.02 shows. Click-outs come next. Below about 21,000 click-outs a week for two weeks the severe case applies, and any offer is then compared with a run-off, as Exhibit 3.23 sets out.

The answer turns on search revenue after 2027 and on the partner's terms.

Not without help.

Cash falls below the $2.5M test in December, as Exhibit 6.10 shows. The plan asks for a commitment of up to $3.5M of repaid-first money, and three levers can bring the amount used down to about $0.9M, as Exhibit 6.01 shows. Ownership needs about $3.8M, as Exhibit 6.02 shows.

It depends on what search revenue does after 2027.

A sale returns more if search revenue keeps falling, and ownership returns more if it holds, as Exhibit 4.12 shows. The plan keeps both ready and chooses on 22 January, when the readings, the offers and the tested plan are in hand.

Search revenue would have to fall by less than about 6% a year on today's team.

With the team down to six the break-even is a fall of about 10% a year. The record is a fall of 23% to 28% a year, so the fall has to slow sharply after 2027, as Exhibit 5.05 and Exhibit 5.06 show.

Five stop rules, read every quarter.

Exhibit 5.13 sets them out. If search keeps falling and the lenders stop at the first review, Comvest gets back about $9.6M to $11.5M, as Exhibit 5.08 shows. That is less than a sale in March.

Separation removes most of the cost, and AI a smaller part.

Exhibit 3.08 walks from head-office cost to a core of six. About six to nine people's work remains in testing, review, partners and judgement, and roles change only after the new way of working is proved.

At a small size, about.

Its loss is its overhead, and its repeat business makes money, as Exhibit 6.07 shows. A unit of about six people serving existing patients would about break even, as Exhibit 6.08 shows. No roster or quote supports that yet, so a 60-day test comes first.

They are served on each route.

Tests in progress, paid orders, therapy support, claims and records are funded before any pay-out to the lenders. Exhibit 6.25 sets out the cap on Sleep Care's cash and the duties it keeps.

Most of the first steps need nothing signed by the borrower.

Counsel reads the signed loan documents, and rights are reserved.

An information wall goes around the Saatva credit, and the company supplies bank statements and confirms the domain renewal. None of it needs anything signed by the borrower. The first three decisions in Exhibit 6.05 cover it.

Lenders holding a majority of the loan, against a rule adopted before offers arrive.

They decide on a paper from the board's independent officer and the banker. Exhibit 3.11 sets out the three questions the rule asks, and Exhibit 3.10 shows the minimum price by what ownership would do.

An operator chosen by the lenders, above today's general manager, answering to a board of three.

The lenders set the stop rules, the funding and the final sale. Exhibit 6.24 sets out who decides what, and Exhibit 6.06 lists the six conditions met before the lenders choose to operate.
